titre: The Hanoi Rat Massacre, or the Incentive That Rewarded the Tail
accroche: In 1902, Hanoi pays one cent per rat tail turned in. Three months later, the city has more rats than before.
contenu_vulgarise:
In April 1902, the French colonial authorities in Hanoi announce a bounty of one cent per rat tail brought to the administration. The city has just acquired a brand-new sewer system, more than 19 kilometers built beneath the French Quarter in the Western manner, and this network, with no predators or obstacles, has turned into a rat superhighway, with rats climbing at night into the most fashionable apartments. The Vietnamese sewer workers, charged with the hunt, having gone on strike in the face of the task, the administration chooses to subcontract the problem to the entire population, for pay.

## The Mechanism: A Bounty That Rewards the Tail, Not the Death

The result exceeds all expectations. At the end of April, nearly 8,000 tails are turned in per day; on June 21, the peak reaches more than 20,000 in a single day. But the administration soon notices tailless rats, very much alive, still moving through the sewers. The bounty was on the cut tail, not the dead rat: hunters were therefore releasing the animals after mutilating them, so that they would breed and supply new tails to cash in. Inspectors even discover clandestine farms kept for the sole purpose of producing tails, as well as a network bringing rats from all over Tonkin to Hanoi to sell them on the spot.

The historian Michael Vann, who unearths the episode in the colonial archives for a landmark article published in 2003, sees in it a textbook case of what economics today calls a perverse incentive: a reward that, by measuring an indicator instead of the real objective, ends up encouraging exactly what it was meant to fight. The campaign, far from reducing Hanoi's rat population, probably made it grow.

## A Misreading of What a Bounty Measures

The episode has a darker side than the anecdote. The proliferation of rats coincides with the third worldwide plague pandemic, and in 1903 Hanoi records 159 cases of bubonic plague, 110 of them fatal: almost all among the Vietnamese population, against six cases among French colonists. The sewer system, conceived as a sanitary advance, had created the conditions for its own defeat.

The lesson this story gives goes beyond colonization: any public policy that pays on a proxy indicator, rather than on the result it aims for, is exposed to the same reversal, a production quota counted in pieces rather than quality, a poorly chosen numerical target in a contemporary administration. What Hanoi illustrates best is that the difficulty is almost never in wanting to do good, but in choosing what we agree to count in place of what we are really after.

repere.texte: Between the end of April and June 21, 1902, the number of rat tails turned in each day to the Hanoi administration rises from about 8,000 to more than 20,000, without the rat population shrinking.

carte.punch: Hanoi, 1902: paying a bounty per rat tail made rats more numerous.
carte.idee: In April 1902, Hanoi's colonial administration pays one cent per rat tail to clear the city's new sewers. Hunters quickly realize it is enough to cut off the tail and release the rat so that it breeds and supplies more.
carte.source_courte: M. Vann, The Great Hanoi Rat Hunt, 2018

quiz.question: Why did the rat bounty introduced in Hanoi in 1902 fail to reduce their population?
choix: Because it rewarded the cut tail, which led some to release mutilated rats so that they would breed
Because the campaign's budget ran out within the first few weeks
Because the rats took refuge outside the sewers, where hunters could no longer reach them
Because the administration ended up suspending the hunt for fear of an epidemic
quiz.explication: The bounty was on the tail, not the dead rat: cutting off the tail and releasing the animal took less effort than killing it, and let the rats breed to supply new tails to cash in, even to the point of genuine clandestine farms.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Why did Hanoi's administration entrust the rat hunt to the population rather than to its own agents?
choix: Because the administration's budget no longer allowed it to pay full-time agents
Because the population had asked to take part in the campaign for extra income
Because the Vietnamese sewer workers charged with the hunt had gone on strike in the face of the task
Because the sewers were too dangerous for municipal agents to enter
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text specifies that the Vietnamese sewer workers charged with the hunt had gone on strike in the face of the scale of the task, which led the administration to subcontract the campaign to the whole population, for pay.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How many cases of bubonic plague did Hanoi record in 1903, and to what extent did they affect the Vietnamese population?
choix: 159 cases, almost all among French colonists
159 cases, almost all among the Vietnamese population
20,112 cases, split evenly between colonists and the local population
8,000 cases, only among children in poor neighborhoods
